lessons.title: The Original Six
lessons.objective: Name the six teams and understand why they shaped hockey.

payload.prompt: Match each Original Six team to its clue.

pairs.definition: The first U.S. team in the NHL, joining in 1924.
New York's team, playing at Madison Square Garden.
Hockeytown, and home of the octopus-on-the-ice tradition.
Canadian giant whose last Stanley Cup came in 1967.
Montreal's team, with 24 Stanley Cups, the most of any franchise.
Windy City team that won the Cup in 2010, 2013 and 2015.

explanation.summary: From 1942 to 1967 the NHL had exactly these six teams: four in the U.S. and two in Canada. Every one of them is still around today.
explanation.sayThisLine: Original Six night is a big deal, isn't it? Which two are playing?

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: The Canadiens are from Montreal, right? They've been around forever.

payload.question: How would you respond?

options.text: Yes. They began in 1909 and have won more Cups than anyone.
options.explanation: Right. Founded in 1909, the Canadiens are the NHL's oldest active club and lead the league with 24 Cups.

options.text: I think they're from Toronto.
options.explanation: Toronto is the Maple Leafs. Montreal is the Canadiens, who are also called the Habs.

options.text: They joined in 1967 with the expansion teams.
options.explanation: They are one of the Original Six and far older than the 1967 expansion.

payload.translation: Montreal Canadiens, founded in 1909, nicknamed the Habs. Their history is a big part of why fans love them.

followUps.line: Which Cup win is your favorite memory?
followUps.why: Invites her story rather than showing off numbers.

followUps.line: Do you go to games at the Bell Centre?
followUps.why: A warm, curious question about her own experience.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You only need one solid fact, like 1909 or 24 Cups. Then ask her to tell you more.

payload.prompt: Match each Original Six era milestone to its meaning.

pairs.definition: After the Brooklyn Americans stopped playing, six clubs remained.
The NHL doubled to twelve teams and the Original Six era ended.
A quarter-century with the same six clubs, so the same teams met all the time.

explanation.summary: Because the same six teams played each other constantly, every rivalry had decades of history built in. That is why Original Six nights still feel special.
explanation.sayThisLine: It's wild that the league was just six teams for twenty-five seasons.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: The Leafs haven't won the Cup since 1967. Do you know how painful that is?

payload.question: What is she telling you?

options.text: Toronto's last title came in 1967, the last Original Six year, and fans are still waiting.
options.explanation: Right. The Leafs' last Cup came in 1967, nearly six decades of waiting, which is why Toronto fans carry so much feeling.

options.text: Toronto has never won a Stanley Cup.
options.explanation: They have won thirteen. The pain is that the last one was so long ago.

options.text: Toronto only plays in the Original Six now.
options.explanation: The league has 32 teams. She is talking about a title drought, not a schedule.

payload.translation: Toronto has not won a Stanley Cup since 1967. Their fans feel that long drought a lot.

followUps.line: Which season did it feel closest?
followUps.why: Lets her share a real memory, which is better than a stat.

followUps.line: Is the playoff hope different this year?
followUps.why: Turns sympathy into a forward-looking question.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Be gentle with a drought. Let her tell you where it hurts.

payload.prompt: The Pittsburgh Penguins are one of the Original Six.

scene.alt: A list of six old NHL team names.

explanation.correct: False. Pittsburgh joined in 1967, one of the six teams added when the league doubled. The Original Six are Boston, Chicago, Detroit, Montreal, New York and Toronto.
explanation.incorrect: The Penguins joined in the 1967 expansion. The Original Six are Boston, Chicago, Detroit, Montreal, New York (Rangers) and Toronto.

lessons.title: Expansion and Sun Belt Hockey
lessons.objective: Explain how the NHL grew from six teams to 32.

payload.prompt: Order the major NHL expansion waves.

items.text: 1967: Six becomes twelve. Los Angeles, Philadelphia, Pittsburgh and St. Louis arrive.
items.why: The Original Six era ends as the league doubles in size.

items.text: 1970-1979: Vancouver, Buffalo, Atlanta, Washington and four teams from the WHA join.
items.why: Steady growth in the decade that followed, including the 1979 merger with the rival WHA.

items.text: 1991-2000: San Jose, Tampa Bay, Florida, Nashville, Columbus and more arrive.
items.why: Hockey pushes into the U.S. South and other new markets.

items.text: 2017-2021: Vegas and Seattle arrive, bringing the league to 32 teams.
items.why: The modern league finishes at 32. Utah took over Arizona's team in 2024 without adding a team.

explanation.correct: Nice read. The league grew in waves: a big doubling in 1967, steady growth after, then a southern push in the 1990s and two recent additions.
explanation.incorrect: Think in waves: 1967 doubling first, then the 1970s, then the 1990s push into new markets, then Vegas and Seattle.
explanation.sayThisLine: The league started with six teams. Now there are 32 from coast to coast.

payload.prompt: What drove the NHL's big 1967 expansion?

options.text: The wish to reach new U.S. cities and win a U.S. television audience.
Players demanded higher salaries.
Ice rinks became cheaper to build.

explanation.correct: Right. The six-team league wanted American markets and TV exposure, which is why cities like Los Angeles and Philadelphia got teams.
explanation.incorrect: The 1967 doubling was about growth: new American cities, new arenas and a bigger TV audience.
explanation.sayThisLine: Before 1967 every team sat in the northeast, the Midwest or Canada. Then California joined.

payload.prompt: Match each expansion chapter to what it means.

pairs.definition: Six new franchises at once, all in U.S. cities.
Teams in warm-weather cities like Tampa, Florida, Dallas and Las Vegas.
Seattle joined in 2021, and Utah took over Arizona's team in 2024.

explanation.summary: The NHL began as a northern league and grew into a continental one, with teams in places where ice is not a given.
explanation.sayThisLine: Hockey in Florida or Vegas? It turns out that works.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: Vegas won the Cup in only their sixth season. How is that even possible?

payload.question: What is she marveling at?

options.text: A brand-new team won the title far faster than almost any other.
options.explanation: Right. Vegas joined in 2017 and won the Cup in 2023, a very quick rise for an expansion team.

options.text: Vegas won the Cup in its very first season.
options.explanation: They reached the final in year one but lost. The Cup came in their sixth season.

options.text: The Cup has become easy to win.
options.explanation: It is still the hardest trophy in hockey. Her point is how unusual Vegas's rise was.

payload.translation: Vegas went from a brand-new franchise to Stanley Cup champions in six seasons. Most expansion teams take much longer.

followUps.line: Didn't they reach the final in their very first year?
followUps.why: A real fact that shows you know the story.

followUps.line: What was it like watching a young team get that good?
followUps.why: Asks for her experience, not a stat.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If you only know the headline, ask her how it felt. That is better than guessing at details.

payload.prompt: Complete the expansion timeline.
payload.template: The NHL doubled from six to {{twelve}} teams in 1967, and Seattle's arrival in 2021 made it {{now}} teams.

explanation.correct: Right. Six doubled to twelve in 1967, and Vegas (2017) and Seattle (2021) took the league to 32.
explanation.incorrect: The doubling made twelve teams, and Seattle was the newest addition at 32.

lessons.title: Legends and Eras
lessons.objective: Talk about Gretzky, Orr, Lemieux, Crosby and other all-time greats.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: Gretzky's assist record is nuts. Do you think anyone will ever touch it?

payload.question: What would you say?

options.text: Probably not. His assist and points totals are so far ahead that they may never fall.
options.explanation: Right. Gretzky has far more career assists and points than anyone, which is why fans call those records untouchable.

options.text: Of course. Sports records are broken all the time.
options.explanation: Some records fall, but Gretzky's assist total is so far clear that it is rarely considered within reach.

options.text: Ovechkin already broke it.
options.explanation: Ovechkin passed Gretzky's career goals record in 2025, not his assists or points.

payload.translation: Wayne Gretzky finished with 1,963 career assists and 2,857 points, totals that are far beyond anyone else's.

followUps.line: Who is the closest anyone has come?
followUps.why: Invites her to compare eras, which fans love doing.

followUps.line: Did you ever see him play?
followUps.why: A human question that can unlock a real story.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You do not need exact numbers. 'Far ahead of everyone' is honest and enough.

payload.prompt: Match each legend to what he is known for.

pairs.definition: 1970s defenseman who rushed the puck like a forward; the only defenseman to win a scoring title.
The Great One; owns the career records for assists and points.
Pittsburgh superstar who beat cancer in 1993 and kept starring.
The Next One; three Stanley Cups with Pittsburgh and Olympic gold.

explanation.summary: Each era has its superstar, and fans love arguing about them. Orr changed what a defenseman could do, Gretzky and Lemieux ruled scoring, and Crosby carried the torch.
explanation.sayThisLine: Who's your all-time favorite? I'm still learning the eras.

payload.prompt: Who is nicknamed 'The Great One'?

options.text: Wayne Gretzky
Mario Lemieux
Bobby Orr
Sidney Crosby

explanation.correct: Yes. The Great One is Gretzky, whose scoring totals were unlike anyone else's. Lemieux was known as Le Magnifique and Crosby as The Next One.
explanation.incorrect: The Great One is Wayne Gretzky. Lemieux was nicknamed Le Magnifique, and Crosby was called The Next One when he arrived.
explanation.sayThisLine: When someone says 'The Great One', they mean Gretzky.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: They called Crosby 'The Next One' when he was a teenager. Did he live up to it?

payload.question: How would you answer?

options.text: Yes. Three Cups, Olympic golds and years of elite play for Pittsburgh.
options.explanation: Right. Crosby has three Stanley Cups, two Olympic golds for Canada and years at the top of the game.

options.text: No. He never won anything.
options.explanation: He has won a lot, including three Stanley Cups.

options.text: It is only a nickname, so it means nothing.
options.explanation: The nickname carried real pressure because it compared him to Gretzky.

payload.translation: 'The Next One' was a label for Crosby's huge expectations as a teenager. He backed it up with three Stanley Cups and Olympic gold.

followUps.line: Who would you say is the next generation's star?
followUps.why: Moves her toward modern names like McDavid.

followUps.line: Where were you for the 2010 Olympic final?
followUps.why: Invites a memory tied to one of his biggest moments.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: A quick fact plus a question beats a long speech.

payload.prompt: Gretzky still holds the NHL career goals record.

explanation.correct: False. Alex Ovechkin passed Gretzky's 894 career goals in 2025. Gretzky still owns the assist and points records.
explanation.incorrect: Ovechkin broke the goals record in 2025, passing Gretzky's 894. Gretzky's assist and points records still stand.

lessons.title: Miracle on Ice and the Golden Goal
lessons.objective: Explain iconic moments that defined hockey.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: The Miracle on Ice was the U.S. beating the Soviet Union in 1980. Everyone still talks about it.

payload.question: Why is that such a big deal?

options.text: The Soviets were the dominant team, and a young U.S. college team beat them.
options.explanation: Right. The Soviet team had won the four Olympics before 1980, and the U.S. roster was mostly college players.

options.text: It was just a normal round-robin game.
options.explanation: It was the medal round, and a huge upset on top of that.

options.text: The U.S. had never won an Olympic hockey medal before.
options.explanation: The U.S. had medaled before, including gold in 1960. The shock was beating the Soviets.

payload.translation: In 1980 a U.S. team of college players beat the powerhouse Soviet team in the medal round, then beat Finland to win gold.

followUps.line: Did the U.S. win gold after that game?
followUps.why: Yes, they beat Finland two days later.

followUps.line: Have you seen the game or the movie?
followUps.why: Lets her share the moment as a story.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If you only know the movie version, say so. She will probably love telling you more.

payload.prompt: Match each iconic moment to its story.

pairs.definition: A U.S. team of college players upset the Soviet Union, then won gold.
Sidney Crosby scored in overtime to give Canada men's Olympic gold at home.
Gold in 2018 after a shootout and in 2026 after overtime, both over Canada.

explanation.summary: Each moment is an Olympic game that went down to the wire. Fans still describe exactly where they were for them.
explanation.sayThisLine: Where were you when Crosby scored the Golden Goal?

payload.prompt: Who scored the Golden Goal for Canada in 2010?

options.text: Sidney Crosby
Connor McDavid
Wayne Gretzky

explanation.correct: Right. Crosby scored in overtime against the U.S. in Vancouver. McDavid was only a teenager then, and Gretzky had long since retired.
explanation.incorrect: It was Sidney Crosby, in overtime against the United States at the 2010 Games in Vancouver.
explanation.sayThisLine: Crosby's overtime goal in Vancouver is Canada's Golden Goal.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: The 2026 Olympics were wild. Both U.S. teams beat Canada in overtime for gold.

payload.question: What does that mean?

options.text: The U.S. women and men both won gold, each over Canada in overtime.
options.explanation: Right. Both gold-medal games against Canada went to overtime and the U.S. won each one.

options.text: Canada swept both gold medals.
options.explanation: It was the other way around. The U.S. won both.

options.text: The two U.S. teams played each other in the final.
options.explanation: Men and women play in separate tournaments. Each team faced Canada.

payload.translation: At the 2026 Olympics, the U.S. beat Canada in overtime in both the women's and men's gold medal games.

followUps.line: Which game was harder to watch, the women's or the men's?
followUps.why: Asks for her reaction and shows you know there were two games.

followUps.line: Did you watch them live?
followUps.why: A warm opening to a story.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If you followed one game more than the other, say so. She will like the honesty.

payload.prompt: Complete the Miracle on Ice story.
payload.template: In 1980 the U.S. beat the {{rival}} in the medal round, then beat {{final}} for gold.

explanation.correct: Right. The big upset was the Soviet Union, and Finland was the final that made it gold.
explanation.incorrect: The upset was over the Soviet Union, and the U.S. still had to beat Finland to win gold.

lessons.title: Rivalries
lessons.objective: Explain a few classic rivalries and why they matter.

payload.prompt: Match each rivalry to its story.

pairs.definition: Original Six rivals with one of the most-played playoff matchups ever.
The Canada-versus-Canada Original Six rivalry.
The Battle of Alberta, between Edmonton and Calgary.
Crosby versus Ovechkin, and a run of big playoff series in the 2010s.

explanation.summary: Rivalries come from history, geography or stars. They turn an ordinary date on the schedule into an event.
explanation.sayThisLine: Is it the Battle of Alberta tonight? That's a real one.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: Whenever the Bruins play the Canadiens, it feels different. Like it matters more.

payload.question: Why is that?

options.text: They are old Original Six rivals with decades of big playoff series.
options.explanation: Right. Bruins-Canadiens carries decades of history, so even a regular-season game comes with extra weight.

options.text: The teams always finish next to each other in the standings.
options.explanation: Rivalries are about history, not standings position.

options.text: The rule book is different when they play.
options.explanation: The rules never change. The feeling comes from the history between the clubs.

payload.translation: Old rivalries bring history with them, so the game feels bigger than two points in the standings.

followUps.line: Do you remember a great one between them?
followUps.why: Invites her memory, not your knowledge.

followUps.line: Is the playoff version even louder?
followUps.why: Shows you know playoffs raise the stakes.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: A rivalry is a story she loves. Ask her for it.

payload.prompt: Match each rivalry type to an example.

pairs.definition: Two nearby cities, like Edmonton and Calgary.
Decades of big series, like Bruins-Canadiens.
Built on two stars, like Crosby and Ovechkin in the 2010s.

explanation.summary: Rivalries come from location, history or stars. The best ones mix all three.
explanation.sayThisLine: The best rivalries mix history, location and star power.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: Why does everyone get so worked up about this one game? It's the same as any other.

payload.question: How would you explain it?

options.text: Rivalries carry history, so the game means more than the two points.
options.explanation: Right. Past series, near neighbors and star duels give a rivalry game a weight a normal game does not have.

options.text: It is just marketing.
options.explanation: Marketing plays up rivalries, but fans feel them because of real history.

options.text: All games are exactly the same.
options.explanation: The standings value is the same, but the feeling in the building is not.

payload.translation: A rivalry game carries the memory of past games, so it feels bigger than the standings suggest.

followUps.line: Do you have a rivalry you love?
followUps.why: Turns explanation into her story.

followUps.line: Have you ever been to one in person?
followUps.why: Those games are famously loud.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Rivalries are fun and friendly when you keep them about the game, not the people.

payload.prompt: What usually turns an opponent into a rival?

options.text: Playoff history, nearby cities or a star-versus-star story.
Wearing similar jersey colors.
Having the same number of points.
Playing in the same time zone.

explanation.correct: Yes. Rivalries are built on shared history, geography and stars, not on colors or standings.
explanation.incorrect: Rivalries grow from history and competition: big playoff series, nearby cities and stars who keep facing each other.

lessons.title: Hats, Beards, Octopi and the Cup
lessons.objective: Explain rink traditions and why fans love them.

payload.prompt: Match each rink tradition to its story.

pairs.definition: After a player's third goal, fans throw hats onto the ice.
Began in 1952, when eight wins won the Cup, one per tentacle.
Players stop shaving for the whole playoff run, for luck.
After a playoff series, both teams shake hands.

explanation.summary: Hockey's traditions are small rituals that fans and players share. They connect one generation of fans to the next.
explanation.sayThisLine: I heard about the hats and the octopus. Which one is your favorite?

payload.prompt: What happens to the Stanley Cup after the final?

options.text: Winning players and staff each get time with it over the summer.
It is locked away in an NHL office until next season.
It is melted down and remade each year.

explanation.correct: Right. Each member of the champion gets a day with the Cup, which travels with a keeper. It has been to hometowns, rinks and all sorts of surprising places.
explanation.incorrect: The Cup is not locked away or melted. It travels over the summer with a keeper, and winners take turns celebrating with it.
explanation.sayThisLine: I love that every winner gets a day with the Cup.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: I saw a photo of someone's dog eating from the Stanley Cup. Is that allowed?

payload.question: How would you explain it?

options.text: Winners get a day with it and often share it with family, dogs and all.
options.explanation: Right. The Cup is treated with respect but is also very much shared. Winners often celebrate with friends and family, pets included.

options.text: No. Only the captain is allowed to touch the Cup.
options.explanation: Every player lifts it, and the winners share it widely.

options.text: That photo must be fake because nobody is allowed near it.
options.explanation: It is a real tradition, though a keeper travels with the Cup.

payload.translation: The Stanley Cup is treated with respect but is shared with winners' families and friends. Some of those celebrations are silly.

followUps.line: If you got a day with the Cup, where would you take it?
followUps.why: Playful and invites her imagination.

followUps.line: Did you ever see it in person?
followUps.why: A warm question about her own experience.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If you are unsure about a detail, enjoy the story and ask her for hers.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: What's the All-Star Game? Is it like the All-Star break in other sports?

payload.question: How would you explain it?

options.text: It is a mid-season showcase of the league's stars, played for fun.
options.explanation: Right. The All-Star weekend is a showcase with a friendly game and skills contests. Nothing in the standings changes.

options.text: It decides the league's regular-season champion.
options.explanation: It has no effect on standings. The regular-season winner is decided by points.

options.text: It is an amateur tournament for college players.
options.explanation: The players are the NHL's own stars.

payload.translation: The All-Star weekend is a celebration with a friendly game and skills contests. It is about fun, not points.

followUps.line: Which skills contest do you like best?
followUps.why: Shows you know the weekend has more than one event.

followUps.line: Who would you pick as the face of the game right now?
followUps.why: Invites her opinions on current stars.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: The format changes from year to year, so ask her what she remembers.

payload.prompt: Fans throw hats onto the ice after any goal.

scene.alt: Hats scattered on the ice after a goal.

explanation.correct: False. Hats come out for a hat trick, a player's third goal in a game. Throwing one after a normal goal is just wasting a good hat.
explanation.incorrect: The hat tradition is for a hat trick, when one player scores three goals in a game.

lessons.title: Hockey Slang and Chirping
lessons.objective: Decode the slang fans use and understand the etiquette of talk.

payload.prompt: Match each slang term to its meaning.

pairs.definition: The puck. 'He put the biscuit in the basket' means he scored.
A slick stickhandling move that beats a defender.
A saucer pass that lifts off the ice and lands flat on a stick.
A shot that hits the underside of the crossbar and goes in.

explanation.summary: Slang is half the fun of hockey talk. You will hear all of these from fans who love the game.
explanation.sayThisLine: That dangle was filthy. Put it bar down, too.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: He dangled three guys and buried it bar down. That was nasty.

payload.question: What just happened?

options.text: A player stickhandled past three defenders and scored off the crossbar.
options.explanation: Right. Dangled means beat defenders with stickhandling, buried means scored, and bar down means in off the crossbar. Nasty here is a compliment.

options.text: A player hit three opponents and got a penalty.
options.explanation: Dangling is stickhandling, not hitting. Nothing in her line is a penalty.

options.text: A goalie made three saves and then got injured.
options.explanation: Buried it means the puck went into the net.

payload.translation: A player beat three defenders with stickhandling and scored off the crossbar. She loved it.

followUps.line: Was that in person or on TV?
followUps.why: A warm question that keeps her story going.

followUps.line: Was it the best goal you've seen this year?
followUps.why: Invites her opinion.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If a slang word loses you, ask. 'What does that one mean?' is a great question.

payload.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.

pairs.definition: Friendly trash talk between players, like jokes and teasing.
Players shake hands after a playoff series, however heated it was.
Teasing is fine, but attacking someone's family or identity is not.

explanation.summary: Chirping is part of hockey culture, but it has a code. Heat on the ice, respect off it.
explanation.sayThisLine: Chirping is part of the fun, as long as it stays on the right side of the line.

payload.title: Decoding a chirp
payload.setting: You watch a game together and she laughs at two players talking during a stoppage.

exchanges.theirMessage: Did you see those two? They're chirping each other like crazy.

replies.text: Is that normal? I thought they'd be fighting.
replies.theirResponse: It's normal. It's trash talk, and most of it is pretty funny.
replies.coachNote: You asked honestly and showed you knew the difference between chirping and fighting.

replies.theirResponse: It can sound that way, but it's part of the game.
replies.coachNote: Honest, but she probably wants you curious, not judging.

replies.text: Whoever wins the fight wins the argument.
replies.coachNote: Hockey is not all fighting; do not reduce it to that.

exchanges.theirMessage: They'll probably laugh about it later.

replies.text: So it's heat on the ice, respect off it?
replies.coachNote: You captured the unwritten rule in your own words.
Polite, but it leaves the conversation flat.

replies.text: I bet they really hate each other.
replies.coachNote: Assuming real hatred misses how playful it usually is.

payload.closingNote: Chirping is banter with a code: tease hard, then show respect.

payload.prompt: Complete the goal slang.
payload.template: A shot through the goalie's legs goes {{hole}}, and one into the upper part of the net goes {{shelf}}.

explanation.correct: Right. Five-hole is the gap between the goalie's pads, and top shelf is the high part of the net where pucks are hardest to stop.
explanation.incorrect: Five-hole is between the goalie's legs. Top shelf is the upper part of the net, near the crossbar.
explanation.sayThisLine: Top shelf! That's where mama hides the cookies.
